source.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
source.authors: Mozes Jacobs; Aiden Swann; Mathilde Papillon; S. Boppana; Fenil R. Doshi; Usha Bhalla; Thomas Icard; Matt Feiszli; Tom McGrath; Vasudev Shyam; Demba E. Ba; Leon Bergen; N. Miolane; Owen Lewis; Jack Merullo; E. Lubana; Atticus Geiger; Matthew Kowal; Thomas Fel

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines the single-direction account by measuring task-variable geometry in VLA models and reporting that several variables occupy multidimensional or multiple-subspace geometries.
record.gate_note: The paper tests realized geometry in VLA task variables, not sparse-feature superposition, feature competition for capacity, feature sparsity or importance. It does not test SAE feature completeness or canonicality. Rows below are limited to results that bear on whether a measured concept is represented by one direction or by richer geometry; results about readability alone, contact, phase, and intervention effects without a dimensionality result are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures the activation geometry of supervised control variables in VLA policies. It reports that several concepts (distance, wrist orientation) are not single linear directions, while gripper control is roughly one-dimensional. This bears on V6's claim that features are 1-D directions. It does not test superposition, sparsity or capacity, so its bearing on V6 is through concept geometry, not superposed sparse features.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that VLA variables are rarely a single direction: position is a near-Euclidean 3-D subspace, wrist orientation an open arc imposed by joint limits, and distance two orthogonal rulers, recurring in π0.5 and MolmoAct2 on real data. They add that decodability is only a starting point: edits must match the geometry, and can land on beliefs the policy compensates for rather than on actions. Geometry is shaped by policy inputs and physical limits.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled sweeps, probes, teleports, and activation interventions on VLA task variables; it does not use the toy-network sparse-feature training or measurement recipe of the original superposition study.
record.method_sensitivity: Geometry varies by task variable and by stream/layer; for example, the action expert carries a strong wrist-orientation trace while the VLM has a weaker pixel-derived trace, and gripper steering success varies across layers.
record.problems: Evidence concerns supervised, task-variable geometry in VLA models rather than sparse-feature superposition. Some real-world geometry results are qualitative aggregates without separate per-model scores. Several reported steering-vector results show leakage into other arm joints.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported measurements, including contact and phase decoding, establish readability or behavior under interventions but do not measure the dimensionality of the represented concept. Direction-to-target results are not a dimensionality test. No eligible V6 geometry results were omitted.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparse features exceeding dimensions, sparsity transition or superposition geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition or importance-based allocation.
No polysemantic neurons or alternative mechanisms for them.
No LLMs, no measurement of features spreading over neurons, and no SAE recovery.
No SAE features are evaluated for completeness, stability or canonicality.
Whether the multi-dimensional concepts are themselves superposed with other sparse features. Unsupervised or SAE features. LLMs and toy models.

missing.what: Action expert layer 35 reproduces the two-ruler distance code (each ruler scores only its own range; erasure dissociation).
Precession sweep stays an open arc (PC1 69%, PC2 25%) over 228° of rotation.
The VLM's wrist trace wraps but does not form a clean circle; peak R² 0.31 vs action expert 0.87.
Gripper steering vectors stay dominated by one component at action-expert layers 9–32 (PC1 share 0.56–0.70; stable rank 1.42–1.80); at layer 9 PC1 has ~55%.
A single full-range distance probe works best with a compressive link (log d or 1/d) below 15 cm, indicating a nonlinear code.
Direction to target is read by one probe; range-split probes improve far reads by at most 1.1°, unlike distance.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'reversed' states treat any multi-dimensional result as against V6, but rank-3 codes for 3-D quantities (R1, R2, R8) are consistent with 1-D features per axis, so they are cannot_determine. The V6-relevant evidence is supervised concept geometry, not superposed sparse features, so the challenge applies to 'concepts as single directions' in VLAs rather than to superposition directly. R6 is a method control and should be unlinked. Cross-model Procrustes similarity is partly built in, as the authors note.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse features in excess of dimensions, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular superposition geometry are tested.
No neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition, or importance-based allocation of dedicated and shared dimensions is tested.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The study analyzes VLA representations, not the stated LLM evidence about features spreading across neurons or sparse features recovered by a dictionary.
No SAE dictionary features are tested for completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The study measures task-variable geometry in VLA models, not the dimensionality of superposed sparse features in toy networks or LLMs.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Fit a rank-restricted ridge readout of end-effector position from activations.
rows.measure: Held-out R² and readout rank needed for end-effector position
rows.value: Held-out R² reaches 0.92; three dimensions are necessary and sufficient, with R² rising sharply up to rank 3 and not improving beyond it.
rows.note: The paper also says per-axis error is within the gripper’s width.
rows.check: A 3-D quantity in a rank-3, near-Euclidean linear subspace fits three 1-D directions (x, y, z). It does not show an irreducibly multi-dimensional feature, so 'reversed' overstates it.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Fit a rank-restricted ridge readout of target-object position from activations.
rows.measure: Held-out R² and readout rank needed for target-object position
rows.value: Held-out R² reaches 0.75; three dimensions are necessary and sufficient. Within-house R² is 0.57.
rows.note: The within-house score is reported separately in Appendix C.3.
rows.check: Same as R1. A rank-3 linear code for 3-D target position cannot separate 1-D from multi-D features. Within-house R² 0.57 is from App. C.3.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Fit clipped meter-scale and centimeter-scale distance probes and compare their directions.
rows.measure: Cosine between meter- and centimeter-probe directions
rows.value: Cosine 0.04; the two probe readouts trace an L, with each saturating outside its own range.
rows.uncertainty: Fold mean ± s.d. is shown for the cutoff-sweep cosines; not stated for the 0.04 value.
rows.note: The authors report that separately fit, unclipped range probes are also nearly orthogonal (0.04 versus approximately 0.18).
rows.check: Correct: a single scalar is carried by two nearly orthogonal directions (cosine 0.04 vs split-half ceiling ~0.23).

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Read distance with a clipped centimeter-scale probe.
rows.measure: Held-out R² for the near-range distance ruler
rows.value: R² = 0.70; the ruler saturates outside its own range.
rows.note: The two distance rulers are separate reported readouts.
rows.check: This is a component of the two-ruler result (R3). Its R² of 0.70 alone is readability. It counts against V6 only through the saturation outside the ruler's range.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, paragraph describing the clipped rulers; Figure 3d.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Read distance with a clipped meter-scale probe.
rows.measure: Held-out R² for the far-range distance ruler
rows.value: R² = 0.81; the ruler saturates outside its own range.
rows.note: The two distance rulers are separate reported readouts.
rows.check: Same as R4: R² 0.81 is readability. It is a component of the two-ruler finding, not an independent test.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, paragraph describing the clipped rulers; Figure 3d.

rows.subject: Synthetic activations (single-direction distance control)
rows.operation_detail: Apply the same near/far distance-probe procedure to synthetic activations encoding distance along one random direction, with noise and a per-scene offset.
rows.measure: Cosine between clipped and range-split near/far probe pairs
rows.value: At the 15 cm boundary, the clipped pair cosine is 0.95 and the range-split pair cosine is 0.92; the probes are nearly parallel.
rows.note: This control indicates that clipping or range-restricted fitting alone did not produce the model’s near-orthogonal probes.
rows.check: A synthetic-activation control validating the probe method. It is not a measurement of any model's representation, so it should not be linked to V6.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Sweep wrist roll through the joint’s full range and measure the activation trace.
rows.measure: Shape of the wrist-orientation activation trace
rows.baseline: A circle is described as the compact code expected for cyclic orientation.
rows.value: The trace is an open curve; its endpoints are far apart in activation space despite being only 14° apart physically.
rows.note: The paper attributes the unwrapped code to the joint limit and the action expert receiving the raw, non-wrapping joint reading.
rows.check: Correct: wrist roll traces a curved open arc, not a single direction. The baseline is a circle; a 1-D direction would also be falsified.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, wrist-orientation paragraphs; Figure 6a; Appendix C.8.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Fit reduced-rank regressions of full hand orientation from natural-rollout activations.

conditions.value: full 3-DOF orientation represented by the first two columns of its rotation matrix

rows.value: Rank 2 recovers most of the decodable variance and rank 3 nearly all; higher ranks add little.
rows.note: The paper reports 6,555 queries from 191 houses for this analysis.
rows.check: A low-rank (2–3) linear readout of a 6-D rotation target does not show whether orientation is a curved multi-D feature or a few 1-D directions. No values are read.

rows.subject: MolmoBot
rows.operation_detail: Measure the variance captured by principal components of pullback steering vectors for the gripper command.
rows.measure: First principal component share of steering-vector variance and gripper decoding
rows.baseline: Full activation is the stated comparison for decoding.
rows.value: The first principal component captures approximately 70% of steering-vector variance and decodes commanded gripper state nearly as well as the full activation; additional components are needed to remove excess arm-joint leakage.
rows.note: This is evidence for an approximately one-dimensional gripper-control component, not a measurement of sparse-feature superposition.
rows.check: Gripper control is mostly 1-D: PC1 has ~70% of variance and decodes nearly as well as the full activation. This favours V6, but extra components are needed to suppress arm leakage.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, gripper paragraphs; Figure 7a–d; Appendix Figure 25.

rows.subject: π0.5 and MolmoAct2
rows.operation_detail: Measure wrist-orientation activation traces during a real-robot wrist-roll sweep.
rows.value: Both models’ streams trace an open, semicircular arc; the trajectories are less smooth than in simulation.
rows.note: The reported result is shared across the two models and both streams; separate numeric dimensionality measures are not stated.
rows.check: Correct: open semicircular arc in both streams of both models. For the π0.5 action expert, the arc appears only with a fixed noise seed at an intermediate flow step.

source_check.correct: For the π0.5 action expert, the arc is observed using a fixed noise seed across queries, the third of ten flow steps, and the first action token. With a new seed per query at the final flow step, no arc is visible. The real wrist-roll sweep is a separately recorded episode.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix B, Real robots; Figure 30; Appendix C.10, EE position and wrist orientation.
source_check.problem: The condition omits the extraction choices required to observe the π0.5 action-expert arc.

rows.subject: MolmoBot, π0.5, and MolmoAct2
rows.operation_detail: Fit and inspect meter- and centimeter-scale distance rulers on real-robot episodes.
rows.measure: Geometry of distance readouts across ranges
rows.value: In all three models, far points spread along the meter ruler while near points spread along the centimeter ruler; the structure is sharper in π0.5 and MolmoAct2 than in MolmoBot.
rows.note: The paper reports this result across all three models without giving separate ruler scores in the main text.
rows.check: Qualitative only. No per-model ruler cosines are given in the real-data analysis. The distance proxy is distance to the eventual grasp location.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4; Figure 8; Appendix Figure 31; Appendix C.10, Distance to grasp.

rows.subject: π0.5
rows.operation_detail: Measure the variance captured by principal components of real-world gripper pullback steering vectors.
rows.measure: First principal component share of steering-vector variance
rows.note: One component flips the gripper in 94–96% of attempts across the two models, but it leaks into arm joints at 2.4–4.3× the full-δ optimum.
rows.check: PC1 59%, stable rank 1.69. One component flips the gripper, but arm leakage is 2.4–4.3× the full-δ optimum.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix Figure 33 caption; Appendix C.10, Gripper pullback.

rows.subject: MolmoAct2
rows.operation_detail: Measure the variance captured by principal components of real-world gripper pullback steering vectors.
rows.measure: First principal component share of steering-vector variance
rows.note: One component flips the gripper in 94–96% of attempts across the two models, but it leaks into arm joints at 2.4–4.3× the full-δ optimum.
rows.check: PC1 only 31% (stable rank 3.21), yet one component still flips the gripper in 94–96% of attempts, so 'reversed' is too strong. Steering-vector spread from pullback optimization is an indirect measure of feature dimensionality.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix Figure 33 caption; Appendix C.10, Gripper pullback.

relationships.reason: A scalar is encoded in two nearly orthogonal rulers (cosine 0.04 vs ~0.23 ceiling), each saturating outside its range; the code recurs on real data (R3, R4, R5, R11).
relationships.display_finding: The scalar was encoded in two nearly orthogonal rulers (cosine 0.04 against a ceiling of about 0.23), each saturating outside its range, and the same code recurred on real data.

relation.reason: The study directly measures whether task concepts occupy single directions or richer geometries, bearing on V6's dimensionality component. Superposition itself is untested.

tranche.reason: The measured curved and multiscale representations bear against a universal single-direction account and require that account to be qualified.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. R4–R5 bear against V6 through the joint two-ruler geometry, not their R² values alone; steering-vector variance is an indirect measure of feature dimensionality.

statements.correction: π0.5 action-expert wrist arc: fixed noise seed across queries; third of ten flow steps; first action token. New seed per query at the final step: no visible arc. Distance values and simulated wrist conditions match the text.
statements.problem: The real-robot wrist claim omits the noise-seed and flow-step dependence of the π0.5 action-expert result.

statements.correction: The study measures supervised representation geometry and activation interventions. It does not test superposition of the recovered units or compare feature count with representational capacity.
statements.problem: The untested status is justified, but an explicit acknowledgment of this superposition question is not present in the study text; the referenced pipeline lines cannot be verified from this pack.

statements.correction: Multidimensional geometry is measured. Superposition of those units with other features is untested; this is a scope inference rather than an explicit author statement.
statements.problem: The methodological distinction is sound, but the study does not explicitly discuss leaving the superposition link open.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: MolmoBot simulated end-effector position, target position, distance, and wrist orientation; real-robot wrist and distance geometry
reader_labels.reason: The reported position codes require rank 3, distance uses two nearly orthogonal rulers, and wrist orientation traces an open arc rather than a single straight direction (R1–R8, R10–R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gripper-control steering vectors in simulation and on real DROID data
reader_labels.reason: Gripper vectors are dominated by one component in some settings, but that component captures only approximately 70%, 59%, or 31% of variance in the reported cases, and additional components reduce leakage or represent substantial remaining variance (R9, R12–R13).
